This product has been focused on CLI interfaces but the system overall needs to be able to handle the full range of user interaction types."

Consumer: the product authority (David). Decision served: whether and how to add a `lead-product-designer` role to the lead shop (alongside lead-pm, lead-po, lead-solutions-architect), what it owns (decision rights), what evidence it admits, how it interfaces with the other three roles, and how it covers every interaction type — CLI, TUI, GUI/web, API and SDK ergonomics, conversational/agent interfaces, voice, notifications/documents — with one consistent user experience.

Scope: industry definitions of the product designer / UX role (Cagan's design owning usability risk; Torres's product trio; Nielsen Norman Group; Norman; IxDA; design-ops); the mechanisms designers use for consistency across interaction types (design systems, design principles, interaction patterns, content/voice guidelines, accessibility standards — WCAG; ISO 9241-210 human-centred design); CLI-specific UX guidance (clig.dev, Heroku CLI style guide, GNU/POSIX conventions, Docker/GitHub CLI design docs, "12 factor CLI"); API/developer-experience design as UX (API design guidelines from Google/Microsoft/Stripe; DX); conversational and agent interface design guidance (e.g. Google conversation design, Nielsen's guidance on AI/agent UX); the designer's relation to PM (value), PO (acceptance), architect (feasibility) and the interfaces among them; designer failure modes.

1	---
2	type: research-report
3	id: product-designer-role-2026-08
4	status: draft
5	version: 5
6	date: 2026-08-25
7	question: "Research a product designer role, which is a gap in this system: the user experience has been left to the PO, architect and the authority, and no role makes it consistent; the product has been CLI-focused but the system must handle the full range of user interaction types."
8	requested-by: product-authority
9	created: 2026-08-25
10	updated: 2026-08-25
11	---
12	
13	# Research report: the product designer role and consistency across every interaction type
14	
15	## Executive summary
16	
17	*How to read the labels.* Each finding carries a confidence: **high** —
18	several sources opened in full agree, at least one primary (the
19	standard, framework, or author itself); **medium** — one opened source,
20	or secondary accounts only (including a paywalled primary carried by an
21	opened secondary — here the report departs from the frame, which
22	labels an unreadable primary low, because the secondary was itself
23	opened and checked; the one case is ISO 9241-210); **low** — recall
24	without a source. "Several" means two or more. "Secondhand" marks a quote taken from a
25	secondary account because the primary was unreachable. Confidence is
26	about the evidence; where a finding predicts an outcome, its likelihood
27	is stated in its own phrase.
28	
29	*How the sources' vocabulary maps to the shop.* Cagan's four risks are
30	value, usability, feasibility, and business viability; his "Product
31	Lead Engineer" (who owns feasibility) is `lead-solutions-architect`;
32	Bob Baxley is Cagan's co-author on the 2025 SVPG essay; `researcher` is
33	the shop's research role, defined in the same six-section form; "the team" and "engineers" are
34	the Bounded Context shops (the shops that each own one Bounded Context,
35	a designed region of the product); an *interaction type* is one way a
36	person or an agent reaches the product — command line (CLI), full-screen
37	terminal (TUI), graphical or web (GUI), API and SDK, conversational
38	(chat), voice, and generated documents or notifications; a *design
39	system* is a governed set of reusable patterns, components, and rules
40	with a named owner; a *scenario* is an acceptance scenario held by a
41	Bounded Context shop's scenario register; a *clarify* is a shop's typed
42	question back to the lead shop. Abbreviations: NN/g — Nielsen Norman
43	Group; SFIA — the Skills Framework for the Information Age, whose level
44	5 is "ensure, advise"; WCAG — the W3C Web Content Accessibility
45	Guidelines, WCAG2ICT its non-web application; AIP — Google's API
46	Improvement Proposals; RACI — the responsibility matrix in which exactly
47	one party is Accountable; HAX — Microsoft's Human-AI Experience toolkit,
48	whose 18 Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction are meant throughout;
49	Grice's Cooperative Principle and "Grice's maxims" name the same
50	linguistic standard; a *definition chain* is the shop's set of linked
51	definitions of good for one artifact type (typedef, guideline, fitness
52	set, process, roles, skill); *external consistency* is NN/g's term for
53	following the conventions of the platform an interface lives on;
54	*local-comprehension* and *knowable-shape* are two of the shop's
55	architecture principles (a part is understandable on its own; the
56	product's shape is knowable from its contracts).
57	
58	1. **The gap is real and has a name: design by committee.** The shop's
59	   present state — experience decided jointly by PO, architect, and
60	   authority, no single owner — matches ProductPlan's definition:
61	   "Design by committee is what happens when multiple parties are
62	   involved in the product design process, and all of their input is
63	   treated equally." Every opened model that names the PM's peers gives usability its own owner: Cagan's
64	   four risks ("The Product Designer is responsible for the usability
65	   risk, and overall accountable for the product's experience — every
66	   interaction our users and customers have with our product"), Torres's
67	   product trio (PM, designer, engineer — "the three roles that — at a
68	   minimum — are required"). The remedy both design-by-committee sources
69	   (Dovetail; ProductPlan) give is one decision-maker deciding on
70	   evidence. *(High.)*
71	2. **The role's scope is medium-neutral by definition, so CLI, API, and
72	   agent interfaces are inside it.** UX "encompasses all aspects of the
73	   end-user's interaction" (Norman & Nielsen); interaction design is "the
74	   conversation between the user and the system" (Cagan & Baxley 2025);
75	   SFIA's user-experience analysis skill (UNAN) covers "a full range of
76	   user tasks not just digital tasks". The CLI guidance corpus (clig.dev, Heroku, GitHub's
77	   Primer CLI) is design guidance in its own right — GitHub files its CLI
78	   design under its design system. *(High.)*
79	3. **What carries consistency across interaction types is not a
80	   component library — it is a small set of governed instruments:**
81	   design principles as decision rules (NN/g, GOV.UK's "consistent, not
82	   uniform"), one vocabulary and voice (Primer "Make it feel like GitHub";
83	   NN/g tone dimensions; the GOV.UK style guide), one core task set that
84	   every interaction type supports (NN/g omnichannel; Google's
85	   conversation design; Alexa "voice-first, but not voice-only"), an
86	   accessibility standard as a cross-cutting constraint (WCAG 2.2 AA;
87	   WCAG2ICT for non-web), and per-interaction-type conventions honoured
88	   as external consistency (NN/g usability heuristic 4, "consistency and standards"; clig.dev "the terminal's
89	   conventions are hardwired into our fingers"). Every mature example
90	   governs these with the same form: criteria + a review body + an
91	   approval state (GOV.UK contribution criteria; Google AIP editors;
92	   Azure's stewardship board). *(High.)*
93	4. **Conversational and agent interfaces have an established external
94	   check and a real paradigm difference.** Microsoft's 18 Guidelines for
95	   Human-AI Interaction are modality-independent; Google's conversation
96	   design rests on Grice's Cooperative Principle; Nielsen classes CLI and
97	   GUI together as command-based (his "command-based interactions"
98	   cover both) and conversational/agent as intent-based
99	   with "reversed locus of control". The designer's
100	   consistency task therefore spans two paradigms, and for generated
101	   interfaces the designer's output becomes "guidance and constraints",
102	   not screens. *(High for the guidance; medium for the paradigm claim and
103	   Nielsen's expectation of hybrid interfaces — one author.)*
104	5. **The agent is also a user.** NN/g: "'user' is no longer synonymous
105	   with 'human'"; Anthropic: invest in the agent-computer interface "just
106	   as much effort" as HCI. Accessibility structure (semantic names,
107	   predictable patterns) and tool/API definitions are the agent's
108	   interface — so API/SDK ergonomics and agent tool contracts sit in the
109	   designer's consistency remit, with the architect owning the contract
110	   itself. *(High — two primary sources opened in full agree; both are
111	   recent, so the practice they describe is young.)*
112	6. **The contested boundary with the PM is known and must be allocated
113	   explicitly.** NN/g's 2021 survey: PMs and UX disagree most on who owns
114	   discovery research (19% of PMs vs 73% of UX say UX), ideation,
115	   information architecture, task flows, the research agenda, and who
116	   explains design to leadership. The recorded failure modes: PMs
117	   "dictate design by sending wireframes to product designers and asking
118	   them to polish them"; the designer as decorator ("pixel-pusher");
119	   hand-off leaving the designer to find requirement gaps. *(High.)*
120	7. **The proposal for `lead-product-designer`** — composed from findings
121	   1–6, a proposal not a finding, so no confidence label; written to the
122	   six-section role form used by `researcher` and
123	   `lead-solutions-architect` — posture; decision rights (decides,
124	   recommends, escalates, never decides); admissible evidence;
125	   interfaces; knowledge and skills; anti-rationalization. *Posture:* one experience across every
126	   interaction type; evidence from users, never opinion; consistent, not
127	   uniform. *Decides (exclusive domain):* the experience guidance corpus
128	   — design principles, vocabulary and voice, the rule that every interaction type supports the same core tasks,
129	   interaction patterns per interaction type, the accessibility target —
130	   and whether a delivered interaction conforms to it. *Decides:* which
131	   interaction type a capability is offered through first — an
132	   experience call, since the PM has already decided the capability is
133	   worth having and the question left is how people reach it; the
134	   information architecture and task flows of every interaction type;
135	   what user research is run and how usability is evaluated. *Recommends:*
136	   to the PM, opportunities and usability findings that change value
137	   judgments; to the PO, acceptance scenarios' usability criteria and
138	   the scenarios that a usability test invalidates; to the architect, the
139	   ergonomics of contracts, CLIs, and agent tool definitions.
140	   *Escalates:* to the authority, a principle the experience corpus cannot
141	   satisfy alongside the architecture principles, and any conflict where
142	   value (PM) and usability pull apart after re-framing. *Never decides:*
143	   what problem is worth solving (PM), acceptance (PO), the stack and
144	   contracts (architect), how a Bounded Context builds a behavior (the
145	   shop). *Admissible evidence:* user tests and trials, prototypes tested
146	   with users, expert review against the corpus, context-of-use analysis,
147	   measured task completion; not admissible — a stakeholder's preference,
148	   a PM-supplied wireframe as a requirement, the designer's own taste
149	   unrecorded. *Interfaces:* PM — framed problems and outcomes in;
150	   usability findings, prototypes, and opportunity evidence out, in
151	   discovery not after it; PO — scenarios in for usability criteria;
152	   usability acceptance criteria and test results out; architect —
153	   contract, CLI, and tool ergonomics reviewed against the corpus;
154	   feasibility and non-functional constraints in; Bounded Context shops —
155	   the corpus and its patterns out; conformance findings back; a
156	   `clarify` on experience questions answered. *Knowledge and skills:* SFIA 9 UNAN, HCEV, USEV, URCH at level 5 ("ensure, advise"); the ISO 9241-210 activities (context of use, user requirements, design solutions, evaluation — secondhand); the HAX guidelines for any agent-facing interaction; WCAG 2.2 AA and WCAG2ICT; clig.dev and Heroku conventions for CLI; Grice's maxims for conversation; the shop's architecture principles (local-comprehension, knowable-shape) as they bear on interfaces.
157	   *Anti-rationalization:* "It's a CLI, developers don't need design" — clig.dev and GitHub say otherwise. "Consistency later" — GOV.UK's contribution criteria gate at publication. "The PM already sketched it" — NN/g's named failure mode. "An agent doesn't care" — NN/g and Anthropic say the agent is a user. "It looks fine to me" — the designer's own preference is not admissible evidence.
158	   *Name:* "product designer" follows the two models the proposal
159	   adopts (Cagan; Torres; Cagan & Baxley); SFIA names skills, not
160	   roles, and its skill names say "user experience"; NN/g's page on
161	   the distinction was unreadable — see 8(c).
162	8. **Two decisions the sources leave to the authority.** (a) Whether the
163	   experience guidance corpus is a new definition type or a principle
164	   set plus guidelines in the existing chain form — the governance
165	   examples fit the existing form. (b) Torres puts usability on the
166	   whole trio ("The trio is jointly responsible for building a
167	   desirable, viable, feasible, usable, ethical product"); Cagan on the
168	   designer alone; the proposal follows Cagan
169	   and RACI (one accountable) with joint discovery. (c) Whether the
170	   role is named `lead-product-designer` or `lead-ux-designer`: the
171	   sources the proposal adopts say "product designer"; the one source
172	   on the naming question was unopened. *(Judgment.)*
173	
174	## Method
175	
176	Three parallel gather workers in fresh contexts covered: the role's
177	definition and interfaces (Cagan/SVPG six essays, Torres two, NN/g
178	seven, SFIA 9 four skills, practitioner sources on failure modes);
179	consistency mechanisms and CLI/API design (NN/g five, GOV.UK four,
180	Atlassian three, W3C two, clig.dev, Heroku, 12-factor CLI via mirror,
181	GitHub Primer CLI via repository source, Docker, Google AIP, Azure
182	guidelines, Stripe two, Textual — a terminal-UI framework's theming guide, the only
183	TUI design document found); conversational and agent interfaces
184	(Google conversation design three pages, Microsoft HAX, NN/g five,
185	Apple WWDC transcript, Alexa two, Google's People + AI Research (PAIR) guidebook two chapters, Shneiderman, Anthropic,
186	OpenAI). About 55 sources opened in full; unreadable: ISO 9241-210
187	(paywalled — principles from a secondary), Material Design 3
188	(JavaScript-rendered), NN/g "UX vs product designer", Apple HIG Siri
189	page (substituted by Apple's own WWDC20 transcript), Amershi et al. full
190	paper (abstract and Microsoft's library used), GOV.UK working-group page
191	(410; Home Office analogue opened). Evidence extracted quotes-first;
192	synthesis; an independent fresh-context verification pass followed.
193	
194	## Findings
195	
196	### F1 — The gap and its name *(high)*
197	
198	- Cagan, "The Four Big Risks" (svpg.com/four-big-risks): "The Product
199	  Designer is responsible for the usability risk, and overall accountable
200	  for the product's experience – every interaction our users and
201	  customers have with our product." PM: "value and viability risks";
202	  engineer: "feasibility risk".
203	- Torres, "Core Concept: The Product Trio" (producttalk.org): "A product
204	  trio is typically comprised of a product manager, a designer, and a
205	  software engineer. These are the three roles that—at a minimum—are
206	  required to create good digital products."
207	- Torres, "Product Trios" (2024): "The trio is jointly responsible for
208	  building a desirable, viable, feasible, usable, ethical product."
209	- ProductPlan, "How to Avoid Design by Committee": "Design by committee
210	  is what happens when multiple parties are involved in the product
211	  design process, and all of their input is treated equally."
212	- Dovetail, "Design By Committee": "a group of designers, stakeholders,
213	  and clients working on the same project and sharing equally valid
214	  opinions"; "In product design, it usually produces low-quality
215	  results"; "you should only have one decision-maker". Riddle and
216	  Treder (UXPin), quoted by ProductPlan: "Committee design is not
217	  collaborative. It's a dictatorship of many".
218	- NN/g RACI (Kaley 2022): "For each task, there should be only one
219	  accountable person."
220	- Cagan 2006, on the absence: "Sometimes the product managers waded into
221	  the design waters and did what they could."
222	
223	### F2 — Scope is medium-neutral *(high)*
224	
225	- Norman & Nielsen, "The Definition of User Experience": "'User
226	  experience' encompasses all aspects of the end-user's interaction with
227	  the company, its services, and its products"; UX ⊃ UI ⊃ usability
228	  ("usability... is a quality attribute of the UI").
229	- Cagan & Baxley 2025: "The product designer is fundamentally responsible
230	  for the user experience of the product. The scope of that
231	  responsibility encompasses the full suite of interactions, touchpoints,
232	  and visual representations — both online and offline";
233	  "Interaction design is the practice of creating and choreographing the
234	  conversation between the user and the system."
235	- SFIA 9 UNAN: "This skill is inclusive of a full range of user tasks not
236	  just digital tasks."
237	- clig.dev: "If a command is going to be used primarily by humans, it
238	  should be designed for humans first"; "The original Macintosh Human
239	  Interface Guidelines recommend 'See-and-point (instead of
240	  remember-and-type)'... These things needn't be mutually exclusive."
241	- Heroku CLI style guide: "The primary goal of anyone developing CLI
242	  plugins should always be usability."
243	- GitHub Primer CLI (repository primer/cli, archived 2024, now under
244	  primer.style/design): "Command line interfaces are not as visually
245	  intuitive as graphical interfaces. They have very few affordances...
246	  We do our best to design our commands to mitigate this."
247	- Stripe (Bu 2020): "Keeping things simple means making sure your APIs
248	  are consistent and predictable"; "creating the right packages to
249	  gradually reveal the power of your API as your users need it."
250	
251	### F3 — What carries consistency, and how it is governed *(high)*
252	
253	- NN/g, Design Principles (Rosala): "Product design principles are value
254	  statements that describe the most important goals that a product or
255	  service should deliver for users and are used to frame design
256	  decisions."; "These principles support consistency in the way
257	  decisions are being made across teams, build confidence in the
258	  decision, and eliminate fruitless debates."; "Be careful that your
259	  principles don't conflict."
260	- GOV.UK Design Principles #9: "Be consistent, not uniform... We should
261	  use the same language and the same design patterns wherever possible.
262	  This isn't a straitjacket or a rule book." #7: "We're not designing for
263	  a screen, we're designing for people."
264	- NN/g heuristic 4: "Systems should adhere to both internal and external
265	  consistency — they should use the same patterns everywhere inside the
266	  system and should also follow web-, platform-, and domain-specific
267	  conventions." clig.dev: "The terminal's conventions are hardwired into
268	  our fingers... that's what makes CLIs intuitive and guessable".
269	- Primer CLI, "Make it feel like GitHub": "Using this tool, it should be
270	  obvious that it's GitHub and not anything else... reflect the
271	  GitHub.com interface as much as possible and appropriate"; "Language
272	  is the most important tool at our disposal for creating a clear,
273	  understandable product."
274	- NN/g tone of voice: "Keep your brand personality consistent, but vary
275	  the tone"; "used when creating writing and other communications for
276	  all channels."
277	- NN/g omnichannel: "Your channel experiences should at minimum support
278	  these core tasks on every channel"; "it's vital... to understand when
279	  it's okay to compromise consistency in order to provide an
280	  appropriately optimized experience on each channel."

282	  store decisions about the user interface."

297	### F4 — Conversational and agent interfaces *(high for guidance; medium for the paradigm claim)*
298	
299	- Google conversation design (the pages carry a notice that
300	  "Conversational Actions were deprecated on June 13, 2023"; the design
301	  guidance outlives the retired product): "a breadth of design expertise (for

303	  design, motion design, and UX writing) that we've refined into a
304	  single discipline"; rests on "Grice's Maxims"; cross-modality rule:

306	  prompt", "they should still convey the same core message".

308	  "Each touch (or remote) target on screen should have a voice command
309	  analog".
310	- Microsoft HAX, 18 guidelines (e.g. G1 "Make clear what the system can
311	  do", G9 "Support efficient correction", G11 "Make clear why the system
312	  did what it did", G17 "Provide global controls"); Amershi et al., CHI
313	  2019, DOI 10.1145/3290605.3300233 (abstract only).
314	- Nielsen, "AI: First New UI Paradigm in 60 Years": "In command-based
315	  interactions, the user issues commands to the computer one at a
316	  time"; generative AI "completely reverses the locus of control";
317	  "Future AI systems will likely have a hybrid user interface".
318	- NN/g, Generative UI: "We must guide the generative UIs, even if we
319	  aren't making minute decisions about individual components."
320	- PAIR: "your users will definitely need a manual failsafe"; AI adds
321	  "context errors" and "background errors". Shneiderman: "high levels of
322	  human control AND high levels of automation."
323	
324	### F5 — The agent as a user *(high)*
325	
326	- NN/g, "AI Agents as Users": "'user' is no longer synonymous with
327	  'human.'"; "Accessibility guidelines achieve this design goal: clear,
328	  descriptive element names, predictable interaction patterns".
329	- Anthropic, "Building effective agents": "plan to invest just as much
330	  effort in creating good agent-computer interfaces (ACI)" as HCI; "Tool
331	  definitions and specifications should be given just as much prompt
332	  engineering attention as your overall prompts."
333	
334	### F6 — The PM boundary and failure modes *(high)*
335	
336	- NN/g, Pernice & Budiu 2021: discovery research — 19% of PMs vs 73% of
337	  UX say UX owns it; IA — "75% of the UXers" say UX, "50% of product
338	  managers" say development; deciding what UX researches — "a clear
339	  example of appropriation".
340	- NN/g, PM archetype 2023: PMs "might try to dictate design by sending
341	  wireframes to product designers and asking them to polish them".
342	- Balsamiq (a wireframing vendor) dissents: "product managers can and
343	  should wireframe" — vendor interest noted; it still proposes a
344	  "Wireframes Contract" under which the PM does not dictate final design.
345	- Marvel (Veen quoted): "Good design isn't [decoration]. Good design is
346	  problem solving."
347	- Torres 2024: "A product manager hands off requirements to a designer.
348	  The designer uncovers gaps in the requirements."
349	- Cagan 2016: designers participate "in all phases of a product, from
350	  discovery to delivery"; "Good product designers use prototypes as
351	  their primary canvas"; "constantly testing their ideas with real
352	  users".
353	- SFIA 9 level 5 (lead level): UNAN "Determines the approaches to be
354	  used for user experience analysis"; USEV "Manages user experience
355	  evaluation... Advises on what to evaluate"; HCEV "Plans and drives user
356	  experience design activities."

358	## Alternatives considered
359	
360	- **Give usability to `lead-pm`.** Cagan's own PM definition excludes
361	  it; NN/g's survey shows the appropriation this produces. Rejected.
362	- **Give it to `lead-po` as acceptance criteria.** Acceptance is a
363	  check, not a definition of good; the check would sit with the same
364	  role that wrote the criteria. Rejected under `define-good-up-front`.
365	- **A per-interaction-type designer (CLI designer, conversation
366	  designer).** Google folded VUI/IxD/visual/writing "into a single
367	  discipline"; the consistency instruments are cross-type. Rejected;
368	  interaction-type conventions become sections of the corpus.
369	- **A design system as a component library first.** No opened source
370	  claims a component library spans CLI/GUI/API; the sources put
371	  principles, vocabulary, and governance first. Deferred.
372	- **Torres's joint accountability for usability.** Compatible in
373	  discovery; RACI and Cagan still require one accountable. The proposal
374	  keeps joint discovery and single accountability.

376	## Limitations

379	  opened secondary and carry medium confidence under the scheme.
380	- No authoritative TUI design guideline exists; TUI guidance would be
381	  derived from clig.dev, WCAG2ICT, and keyboard-first GUI patterns.
382	- The empirical base for failure modes is practitioner writing and one

386	- The paradigm-shift claim (F4) rests on one author.
387	- What would change the judgment: a source showing a single component

# Research report: the product designer role and consistency across every interaction type

## Executive summary

*How to read the labels.* Each finding carries a confidence: **high** —
several sources opened in full agree, at least one primary (the
standard, framework, or author itself); **medium** — one opened source,
or secondary accounts only (including a paywalled primary carried by an
opened secondary — here the report departs from the frame, which
labels an unreadable primary low, because the secondary was itself
opened and checked; the one case is ISO 9241-210); **low** — recall
without a source. "Several" means two or more. "Secondhand" marks a quote taken from a
secondary account because the primary was unreachable. Confidence is
about the evidence; where a finding predicts an outcome, its likelihood
is stated in its own phrase.

*How the sources' vocabulary maps to the shop.* Cagan's four risks are
value, usability, feasibility, and business viability; his "Product
Lead Engineer" (who owns feasibility) is `lead-solutions-architect`;
Bob Baxley is Cagan's co-author on the 2025 SVPG essay; `researcher` is
the shop's research role, defined in the same six-section form; "the team" and "engineers" are
the Bounded Context shops (the shops that each own one Bounded Context,
a designed region of the product); an *interaction type* is one way a
person or an agent reaches the product — command line (CLI), full-screen
terminal (TUI), graphical or web (GUI), API and SDK, conversational
(chat), voice, and generated documents or notifications; a *design
system* is a governed set of reusable patterns, components, and rules
with a named owner; a *scenario* is an acceptance scenario held by a
Bounded Context shop's scenario register; a *clarify* is a shop's typed
question back to the lead shop. Abbreviations: NN/g — Nielsen Norman
Group; SFIA — the Skills Framework for the Information Age, whose level
5 is "ensure, advise"; WCAG — the W3C Web Content Accessibility
Guidelines, WCAG2ICT its non-web application; AIP — Google's API
Improvement Proposals; RACI — the responsibility matrix in which exactly
one party is Accountable; HAX — Microsoft's Human-AI Experience toolkit,
whose 18 Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction are meant throughout;
Grice's Cooperative Principle and "Grice's maxims" name the same
linguistic standard; a *definition chain* is the shop's set of linked
definitions of good for one artifact type (typedef, guideline, fitness
set, process, roles, skill); *external consistency* is NN/g's term for
following the conventions of the platform an interface lives on;
*local-comprehension* and *knowable-shape* are two of the shop's
architecture principles (a part is understandable on its own; the
product's shape is knowable from its contracts).

1. **The gap is real and has a name: design by committee.** The shop's
   present state — experience decided jointly by PO, architect, and
   authority, no single owner — matches ProductPlan's definition:
   "Design by committee is what happens when multiple parties are
   involved in the product design process, and all of their input is
   treated equally." Every opened model that names the PM's peers gives usability its own owner: Cagan's
   four risks ("The Product Designer is responsible for the usability
   risk, and overall accountable for the product's experience — every
   interaction our users and customers have with our product"), Torres's
   product trio (PM, designer, engineer — "the three roles that — at a
   minimum — are required"). The remedy both design-by-committee sources
   (Dovetail; ProductPlan) give is one decision-maker deciding on
   evidence. *(High.)*
2. **The role's scope is medium-neutral by definition, so CLI, API, and
   agent interfaces are inside it.** UX "encompasses all aspects of the
   end-user's interaction" (Norman & Nielsen); interaction design is "the
   conversation between the user and the system" (Cagan & Baxley 2025);
   SFIA's user-experience analysis skill (UNAN) covers "a full range of
   user tasks not just digital tasks". The CLI guidance corpus (clig.dev, Heroku, GitHub's
   Primer CLI) is design guidance in its own right — GitHub files its CLI
   design under its design system. *(High.)*
3. **What carries consistency across interaction types is not a
   component library — it is a small set of governed instruments:**
   design principles as decision rules (NN/g, GOV.UK's "consistent, not
   uniform"), one vocabulary and voice (Primer "Make it feel like GitHub";
   NN/g tone dimensions; the GOV.UK style guide), one core task set that
   every interaction type supports (NN/g omnichannel; Google's
   conversation design; Alexa "voice-first, but not voice-only"), an
   accessibility standard as a cross-cutting constraint (WCAG 2.2 AA;
   WCAG2ICT for non-web), and per-interaction-type conventions honoured
   as external consistency (NN/g usability heuristic 4, "consistency and standards"; clig.dev "the terminal's
   conventions are hardwired into our fingers"). Every mature example
   governs these with the same form: criteria + a review body + an
   approval state (GOV.UK contribution criteria; Google AIP editors;
   Azure's stewardship board). *(High.)*
4. **Conversational and agent interfaces have an established external
   check and a real paradigm difference.** Microsoft's 18 Guidelines for
   Human-AI Interaction are modality-independent; Google's conversation
   design rests on Grice's Cooperative Principle; Nielsen classes CLI and
   GUI together as command-based (his "command-based interactions"
   cover both) and conversational/agent as intent-based
   with "reversed locus of control". The designer's
   consistency task therefore spans two paradigms, and for generated
   interfaces the designer's output becomes "guidance and constraints",
   not screens. *(High for the guidance; medium for the paradigm claim and
   Nielsen's expectation of hybrid interfaces — one author.)*
5. **The agent is also a user.** NN/g: "'user' is no longer synonymous
   with 'human'"; Anthropic: invest in the agent-computer interface "just
   as much effort" as HCI. Accessibility structure (semantic names,
   predictable patterns) and tool/API definitions are the agent's
   interface — so API/SDK ergonomics and agent tool contracts sit in the
   designer's consistency remit, with the architect owning the contract
   itself. *(High — two primary sources opened in full agree; both are
   recent, so the practice they describe is young.)*
6. **The contested boundary with the PM is known and must be allocated
   explicitly.** NN/g's 2021 survey: PMs and UX disagree most on who owns
   discovery research (19% of PMs vs 73% of UX say UX), ideation,
   information architecture, task flows, the research agenda, and who
   explains design to leadership. The recorded failure modes: PMs
   "dictate design by sending wireframes to product designers and asking
   them to polish them"; the designer as decorator ("pixel-pusher");
   hand-off leaving the designer to find requirement gaps. *(High.)*
7. **The proposal for `lead-product-designer`** — composed from findings
   1–6, a proposal not a finding, so no confidence label; written to the
   six-section role form used by `researcher` and
   `lead-solutions-architect` — posture; decision rights (decides,
   recommends, escalates, never decides); admissible evidence;
   interfaces; knowledge and skills; anti-rationalization. *Posture:* one experience across every
   interaction type; evidence from users, never opinion; consistent, not
   uniform. *Decides (exclusive domain):* the experience guidance corpus
   — design principles, vocabulary and voice, the rule that every interaction type supports the same core tasks,
   interaction patterns per interaction type, the accessibility target —
   and whether a delivered interaction conforms to it. *Decides:* which
   interaction type a capability is offered through first — an
   experience call, since the PM has already decided the capability is
   worth having and the question left is how people reach it; the
   information architecture and task flows of every interaction type;
   what user research is run and how usability is evaluated. *Recommends:*
   to the PM, opportunities and usability findings that change value
   judgments; to the PO, acceptance scenarios' usability criteria and
   the scenarios that a usability test invalidates; to the architect, the
   ergonomics of contracts, CLIs, and agent tool definitions.
   *Escalates:* to the authority, a principle the experience corpus cannot
   satisfy alongside the architecture principles, and any conflict where
   value (PM) and usability pull apart after re-framing. *Never decides:*
   what problem is worth solving (PM), acceptance (PO), the stack and
   contracts (architect), how a Bounded Context builds a behavior (the
   shop). *Admissible evidence:* user tests and trials, prototypes tested
   with users, expert review against the corpus, context-of-use analysis,
   measured task completion; not admissible — a stakeholder's preference,
   a PM-supplied wireframe as a requirement, the designer's own taste
   unrecorded. *Interfaces:* PM — framed problems and outcomes in;
   usability findings, prototypes, and opportunity evidence out, in
   discovery not after it; PO — scenarios in for usability criteria;
   usability acceptance criteria and test results out; architect —
   contract, CLI, and tool ergonomics reviewed against the corpus;
   feasibility and non-functional constraints in; Bounded Context shops —
   the corpus and its patterns out; conformance findings back; a
   `clarify` on experience questions answered. *Knowledge and skills:* SFIA 9 UNAN, HCEV, USEV, URCH at level 5 ("ensure, advise"); the ISO 9241-210 activities (context of use, user requirements, design solutions, evaluation — secondhand); the HAX guidelines for any agent-facing interaction; WCAG 2.2 AA and WCAG2ICT; clig.dev and Heroku conventions for CLI; Grice's maxims for conversation; the shop's architecture principles (local-comprehension, knowable-shape) as they bear on interfaces.
   *Anti-rationalization:* "It's a CLI, developers don't need design" — clig.dev and GitHub say otherwise. "Consistency later" — GOV.UK's contribution criteria gate at publication. "The PM already sketched it" — NN/g's named failure mode. "An agent doesn't care" — NN/g and Anthropic say the agent is a user. "It looks fine to me" — the designer's own preference is not admissible evidence.
   *Name:* "product designer" follows the two models the proposal
   adopts (Cagan; Torres; Cagan & Baxley); SFIA names skills, not
   roles, and its skill names say "user experience"; NN/g's page on
   the distinction was unreadable — see 8(c).
8. **Two decisions the sources leave to the authority.** (a) Whether the
   experience guidance corpus is a new definition type or a principle
   set plus guidelines in the existing chain form — the governance
   examples fit the existing form. (b) Torres puts usability on the
   whole trio ("The trio is jointly responsible for building a
   desirable, viable, feasible, usable, ethical product"); Cagan on the
   designer alone; the proposal follows Cagan
   and RACI (one accountable) with joint discovery. (c) Whether the
   role is named `lead-product-designer` or `lead-ux-designer`: the
   sources the proposal adopts say "product designer"; the one source
   on the naming question was unopened. *(Judgment.)*

## Method

Three parallel gather workers in fresh contexts covered: the role's
definition and interfaces (Cagan/SVPG six essays, Torres two, NN/g
seven, SFIA 9 four skills, practitioner sources on failure modes);
consistency mechanisms and CLI/API design (NN/g five, GOV.UK four,
Atlassian three, W3C two, clig.dev, Heroku, 12-factor CLI via mirror,
GitHub Primer CLI via repository source, Docker, Google AIP, Azure
guidelines, Stripe two, Textual — a terminal-UI framework's theming guide, the only
TUI design document found); conversational and agent interfaces
(Google conversation design three pages, Microsoft HAX, NN/g five,
Apple WWDC transcript, Alexa two, Google's People + AI Research (PAIR) guidebook two chapters, Shneiderman, Anthropic,
OpenAI). About 55 sources opened in full; unreadable: ISO 9241-210
(paywalled — principles from a secondary), Material Design 3
(JavaScript-rendered), NN/g "UX vs product designer", Apple HIG Siri
page (substituted by Apple's own WWDC20 transcript), Amershi et al. full
paper (abstract and Microsoft's library used), GOV.UK working-group page
(410; Home Office analogue opened). Evidence extracted quotes-first;
synthesis; an independent fresh-context verification pass followed.

## Findings

### F1 — The gap and its name *(high)*

- Cagan, "The Four Big Risks" (svpg.com/four-big-risks): "The Product
  Designer is responsible for the usability risk, and overall accountable
  for the product's experience – every interaction our users and
  customers have with our product." PM: "value and viability risks";
  engineer: "feasibility risk".
- Torres, "Core Concept: The Product Trio" (producttalk.org): "A product
  trio is typically comprised of a product manager, a designer, and a
  software engineer. These are the three roles that—at a minimum—are
  required to create good digital products."
- Torres, "Product Trios" (2024): "The trio is jointly responsible for
  building a desirable, viable, feasible, usable, ethical product."
- ProductPlan, "How to Avoid Design by Committee": "Design by committee
  is what happens when multiple parties are involved in the product
  design process, and all of their input is treated equally."
- Dovetail, "Design By Committee": "a group of designers, stakeholders,
  and clients working on the same project and sharing equally valid
  opinions"; "In product design, it usually produces low-quality
  results"; "you should only have one decision-maker". Riddle and
  Treder (UXPin), quoted by ProductPlan: "Committee design is not
  collaborative. It's a dictatorship of many".
- NN/g RACI (Kaley 2022): "For each task, there should be only one
  accountable person."
- Cagan 2006, on the absence: "Sometimes the product managers waded into
  the design waters and did what they could."

### F2 — Scope is medium-neutral *(high)*

- Norman & Nielsen, "The Definition of User Experience": "'User
  experience' encompasses all aspects of the end-user's interaction with
  the company, its services, and its products"; UX ⊃ UI ⊃ usability
  ("usability... is a quality attribute of the UI").
- Cagan & Baxley 2025: "The product designer is fundamentally responsible
  for the user experience of the product. The scope of that
  responsibility encompasses the full suite of interactions, touchpoints,
  and visual representations — both online and offline";
  "Interaction design is the practice of creating and choreographing the
  conversation between the user and the system."
- SFIA 9 UNAN: "This skill is inclusive of a full range of user tasks not
  just digital tasks."
- clig.dev: "If a command is going to be used primarily by humans, it
  should be designed for humans first"; "The original Macintosh Human
  Interface Guidelines recommend 'See-and-point (instead of
  remember-and-type)'... These things needn't be mutually exclusive."
- Heroku CLI style guide: "The primary goal of anyone developing CLI
  plugins should always be usability."
- GitHub Primer CLI (repository primer/cli, archived 2024, now under
